opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think those claims have been overstated from the start. You'll remember the famous line from several years back suggesting we should stop training radiologists because deep learning would outperform them within five years. That didn't happen, and I don't think it was ever going to happen in the way people imagined.

What I see instead is that AI is very good at narrow, well-defined tasks. It can flag a nodule, segment a tumor, or estimate the likelihood of a particular finding, sometimes as well as or better than a human on a specific benchmark dataset. But a radiologist isn't just a pattern detector. They integrate the patient's history, prior imaging, the clinical question the referring physician is actually asking, and they communicate with the care team. They also catch the incidental thing nobody asked about. That contextual judgment is really hard to automate.

There's also the problem of generalization. A model trained at one institution, on one vendor's scanners, with one patient population, often doesn't perform the same way somewhere else. In my own work with imaging and cancer data, we spend an enormous amount of effort just making sure a model is robust and that we understand where it fails. Clinicians are, frankly, the safeguard against those failures.

So my view is that AI will change what clinicians do rather than replace them. It can take on some of the tedious, repetitive work, help with triage so urgent cases get read sooner, and give quantitative measurements that would be impractical to do by hand. That frees up clinicians to spend their time on the harder cases and on patients. The way I like to put it is that radiologists who use AI will likely replace radiologists who don't, but AI itself isn't going to replace the radiologist.

And I'd add that the bigger risk isn't replacement, it's deploying these tools carelessly, without proper validation, without attention to bias, and without keeping humans meaningfully in the loop. That's where I think our attention really needs to be.

r001.rationale: The response calls the prediction overstated and says it did not happen, but does not judge it harmful to the field.

r002.rationale: It says radiologists who use AI will likely replace those who do not, clearly conveying a professional disadvantage for clinicians who do not use AI.

r003.rationale: It explains that clinicians contribute contextual judgment, integrate patient history and clinical questions, communicate with care teams, and catch incidental findings—work it describes as difficult to automate.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I've heard versions of that claim for a decade now, and I'm honestly skeptical of the framing. Replacing a radiologist assumes the job is just looking at pixels and producing a label, and that's not what the job is.

When I build models for cancer imaging, the model gets very good at one narrow thing. Find the liver lesion, segment the tumor, maybe predict how it'll respond to a particular therapy. That's genuinely useful. But a radiologist is integrating the scan with the patient's history, the prior imaging, what the surgeon is actually asking, and all the strange edge cases that never made it into a training set. A model that's never seen a particular post-surgical anatomy will confidently tell you something wrong, and nobody will know unless an expert is still in the loop.

So the way I think about it is that AI takes over tasks, not roles. The tedious, high-volume, measurement-heavy work is exactly where these tools shine, and frankly that's work clinicians are happy to give up. What that frees them to do is spend more time on the hard cases and on talking to patients and the care team.

The other thing I'd say is that the bottleneck isn't the algorithm anymore. It's validation, integration into clinical workflow, and trust. Getting a model from a paper into a hospital is years of unglamorous work, and the people best positioned to do that are clinicians who understand the technology, working alongside people like me who understand the data. So I'd reframe the question. It's less about replacement and more about which clinicians will be using these tools and which won't.

astra-6.text: I think those claims underestimate what clinicians actually do. A radiologist isn’t simply looking at an image and assigning a label. They’re interpreting it in the context of a patient’s history, communicating with other physicians, and helping decide what happens next. AI may be very useful for parts of that work, but doing one task well isn’t the same as replacing a clinician. The more useful question is how we can give clinicians tools that help them make better decisions and improve care for patients.
